source.title: Trainable at Depth, Solvable at Small Size: What the Loss Surface of a Polynomial Activation Dictates for Designing, Initializing and Training Networks

record.tranche_reason: The study compares plain and identity-residual networks across depth and reports outcomes, testing whether the shortcut changes deep-network trainability. Its fully connected MNIST setup differs from the convolutional ImageNet and CIFAR settings named in V3.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's plain-versus-residual MNIST depth results. Other reported results, including activation and normalization comparisons, do not test the depth-and-identity-shortcut behavior named by a claim version. The small-model square-loss geometry is not a training-classification-error result.
record.test_reason: The study investigates related optimization questions, but its depth and shortcut comparisons report test accuracy rather than training error. They cannot establish V3's training-error degradation or its prevention. Initialization diagnostics measure gradients before training, and normalization comparisons report final accuracy rather than learning speed or learning-rate tolerance. No supplied result directly tests a claim version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' residual-network conclusion: they interpret the test-accuracy comparisons as showing trainability to depth 300 without normalization and attribute the plain network's failure to clamp saturation. These comparisons do not directly report training-error degradation. Their broader conclusion is that scale control matters more than polynomial activation choice, with projection and identity paths providing different mechanisms.
record.recipe_differences: Fully connected polynomial networks trained on MNIST; compares identity residual connections without normalization rather than batch-normalized convolutional networks with and without shortcuts.
record.method_sensitivity: Depth and initialization affect the plain network's reported outcome; the residual network remains near its depth-10 accuracy through depth 300 in the reported sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: At depths 50–300, plain polynomial networks have approximately chance test accuracy, while identity-residual networks achieve 93.80–94.81%. At depth 100, residual connections substantially improve test accuracy under both initializations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Identity shortcuts preserve useful test accuracy at greater depth in these unnormalized, fully connected polynomial MNIST networks under the fixed training budget.

fits_no_version.finding: At initialization, a depth-30 residual stack has input-gradient norm 5.6569 with a zero-initialized branch versus 30565.2552 at conventional scale; learning speed is not measured.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Zero-initializing this residual branch controls the input-gradient norm before training.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalization comparisons report final test accuracy and gradient ratios; they do not establish faster accuracy gains or tolerance of higher learning rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization changes final test accuracy and depth-dependent performance in the tested fully connected MNIST networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Small polynomial models have computed stationary sets and differing attainable squared losses, without the realizable ReLU teacher-student setup or measured optimization failure frequencies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Projection and residual parametrizations change critical-set geometry and attainable loss in these small polynomial models.

record.problems: The relevant comparisons use fully connected networks on MNIST, not the convolutional ImageNet or CIFAR settings named in V3. Table 5 uses two seeds; Table 4 uses four. The reported classification measure for these comparisons is test accuracy, not training error.
record.rows_left_out: None of the directly relevant plain-versus-residual depth results were left out.

untested.parts: Training classification error of sufficiently large convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, including corrupted labels and the specified size, stopping and regularization conditions.
Spurious-minimum frequencies in realizable two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and their reduction with extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation with depth, persistence under longer training, and prevention by identity shortcuts in the specified convolutional networks; special tanh initializations and Fixup.
Learning speed and trainable depth under activation-matched initializations in plain networks, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and deep orthogonal convolution kernels.
Recovery or divergence relative to a measured stability threshold, curvature dynamics and edge-of-stability training.
Batch normalization's effect on learning speed and learning-rate tolerance, and comparable speed and stability with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: The recorded accuracy values match Tables 4 and 5. Remove both V3 support labels because their evidence measures test accuracy. The architecture and dataset differences further restrict transfer, but are not themselves negative results on V3. No missing directly relevant result is identifiable in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses fully connected networks on clean MNIST labels; it does not test convolutional networks on CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, or the stated early-stopping and regularization conditions.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student experiment or teacher/student width sweep.

The study tests fully connected polynomial networks on MNIST, not batch-normalized convolutional networks on ImageNet or CIFAR-10. It does not test the named special initializations for deep plain tanh networks or Fixup initialization.

The initialization comparison concerns residual-branch initialization, not activation-matched initializations for plain networks, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, or 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
No learning-rate stability threshold, loss-curvature dynamics, or edge-of-stability experiment.
No comparison of batch normalization's training speed or learning-rate tolerance against networks without it, and no Fixup experiment.

rows.operation_detail: Compared a plain polynomial network without normalization or residual connection.
rows.note: The authors say this is above chance but still substantially below the residual arm; the measure is test accuracy.
rows.check: 31.38 ± 11.01% is test accuracy. The initialization is a truncated identity plus random perturbation, rather than an exact identity.

rows.subject: Residual / xavier

rows.note: The authors report a large gain over the no-residual condition; the measure is test accuracy.
rows.check: The increase from 10.99% to 94.50% measures test accuracy, not prevention of training-error degradation.

rows.note: The authors report a large gain over the no-residual condition; the measure is test accuracy.
rows.check: The increase from 31.38% to 93.66% measures test accuracy, not prevention of training-error degradation. Initialization is near-identity.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Fully connected polynomial networks on MNIST at depths 50–300, with Xavier initialization and no normalization
reader_labels.reason: Residual models retain test accuracy around 93.80–94.81% while the plain models are near chance (R3–R8). This supports the shortcut portion in this tested setting, though the measure is test accuracy.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Fully connected polynomial networks on MNIST at depth 100, with Xavier or identity initialization and no normalization
reader_labels.reason: Adding an identity path accompanies a large test-accuracy increase for both initializations (R9–R12).
